items.question: A claims processing manager at a mid-size insurer is redesigning the first-notice-of-loss (FNOL) intake workflow. She has five steps: (1) extract structured fields from the claimant's written statement, (2) cross-check field values against the policy record, (3) generate a preliminary coverage assessment, (4) assign the claim to an adjuster, and (5) notify the claimant that the claim has been received. Which step represents the CLEAREST boundary between Claude-assisted and human-only, and where does it fall?

options.A: After step 1; extraction is Claude-assisted and everything from step 2 onward requires a human
options.B: After step 2; extraction and cross-checking are Claude-assisted, but preliminary coverage assessment and adjuster assignment require human judgment
options.C: After step 5; all five steps are Claude-assisted because they are repeatable processes that follow defined rules
options.D: After step 3; steps 1–3 are Claude-assisted and steps 4–5 are human or system steps

items.question: A legal research analyst at an 18-person litigation boutique evaluates two proposed Claude use cases. Case A: reviewing the same type of contract clause (limitation of liability) across 50 vendor agreements to flag non-standard language. Case B: conducting case-by-case legal research for each active matter, which varies by jurisdiction, theory, and procedural posture. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Case A is higher fit because the task is repetitive with stable criteria; Case B is lower fit because each research task is novel and requires contextual judgment
options.B: Case B is higher fit because legal research is the type of complex task where Claude's language ability adds the most value
options.C: Both cases are equally fit because Claude can handle both document review and research tasks reliably
options.D: Case A is lower fit because contract review requires legal expertise, while Case B is higher fit because research is a text-based task Claude handles well

items.question: An actuarial analyst at a large insurer wants to use Claude in batch mode to draft commentary for the 45 tables in a quarterly reserve report. He plans to run all 45 commentary drafts in a single batch at the start of the week the report is due. A colleague flags a potential problem with this plan. Which problem is MOST likely correct?

options.A: Claude may not produce consistent commentary quality across all 45 tables if they are batched rather than done interactively
options.B: The batch plan assumes all 45 tables are finalised before commentary is drafted; if any tables change after the batch runs, those commentaries become stale and must be redone
options.C: Actuarial commentary requires precise numerical language that Claude cannot produce without a detailed style guide
options.D: Running 45 items in a single batch will likely exceed Claude's output capacity in one session

items.question: A revenue operations lead at a 300-person SaaS company designs a workflow for qualifying inbound leads. The proposal: Claude reads each lead's form submission and company data, assigns a lead score (1–10), writes a personalised outreach email, and places high-scoring leads directly into the sales team's pipeline as "hot." A sales director raises concerns. Which concern identifies the MOST significant design flaw?

options.A: The personalised outreach emails may not match each sales rep's individual voice and style
options.B: Claude's lead scoring is not validated against historical conversion data, so the "hot" classification may not reflect actual deal likelihood
options.C: The form submission data may include incomplete or inaccurate fields that would skew Claude's scoring
options.D: Placing leads directly into the pipeline without sales rep review removes the human judgment that identifies contextual signals not captured in the form data

items.question: A supply chain analyst at a food manufacturer has built a Claude-assisted workflow that drafts weekly supplier performance summaries from a data extract. The summaries have been accurate for three months. This week, the summaries contain incorrect on-time delivery figures that differ from the analyst's own calculations. The analyst has identified two possible causes: (a) the data extract format changed and Claude is reading a different field, or (b) a prompt change made last week altered how Claude interprets the delivery window. What should the analyst do NEXT?

options.A: Rewrite the prompt from scratch to remove any ambiguity about how delivery windows are calculated
options.B: Compare this week's data extract format against last week's to determine whether the source field mapping changed before assuming the prompt is the problem
options.C: Switch from the current Claude tier to a more capable model to improve the accuracy of numerical extraction
options.D: Inform the stakeholders that the summaries are unreliable and pause the workflow until the cause is identified

items.question: A senior editor at a trade publication has been using Claude to flag articles in the editorial queue that exceed the house word limit. This worked well for three months. The workflow now fails to flag an article that is 200 words over the limit. The editor investigates and finds that Claude is counting words differently from the publication's editorial style guide, which excludes captions, pull quotes, and footnotes from the word count. What does this failure MOST clearly illustrate about the original workflow design?

options.A: Claude cannot reliably count words in long documents and should not be used for counting tasks
options.B: The criteria were not fully specified — the prompt defined a word limit but did not define what counts as a word or which text elements are included in the count
options.C: The workflow needed a more capable model to handle the nuanced distinction between body text and ancillary elements
options.D: Word limit enforcement should never be automated and always requires a human editor

items.question: A product operations manager at a software company deploys a Claude-assisted workflow to triage 1,200 monthly bug reports, classifying each as P1 (critical), P2 (significant), or P3 (minor). After two months, the engineering team reports that several P3-classified issues were actually P1 bugs that caused customer-facing outages. The manager reviews the workflow and finds no validation step was built in. What is the MOST accurate description of the root cause?

options.A: The model used was not powerful enough to understand the technical severity of bug reports
options.B: The workflow was deployed at production volume without first validating that Claude's severity classifications matched engineering judgment on a calibration set
options.C: Bug reports are too unstructured and domain-specific for Claude to classify reliably
options.D: The P1/P2/P3 priority framework was not granular enough to capture real severity variation

items.question: A research analyst at an investment bank uses Claude in a single long conversation to analyse a company's 10-K filing (120 pages), then its most recent investor presentation, then three analyst reports, then drafts a 15-page equity research note — all in one session. Midway through the note drafting, the analyst notices that Claude begins contradicting conclusions it drew from the 10-K earlier in the session. What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.A: Claude changed its analysis because newer information in the analyst reports overrode the 10-K findings
options.B: The length of the conversation caused the earliest content (10-K analysis) to fall outside Claude's working context, degrading its ability to maintain consistency with those earlier conclusions
options.C: The investor presentation and analyst reports contained contradictory information that Claude integrated without signalling the conflict
options.D: Claude's reasoning degrades when it is asked to switch between analysis and writing tasks in the same session

items.question: A clinical documentation specialist at a hospital system uses Claude to generate preliminary ICD-10 diagnosis codes from physician notes, with a physician reviewing each code assignment before finalisation. After six months, the quality assurance team reports that the physician review step is taking approximately 45 seconds per encounter — barely faster than coding manually — and the accept-without-change rate is only 52%. The hospital's CMO interprets this as a workflow failure. What does the 52% accept rate MOST likely indicate?

options.A: The physician review step is too long and should be shortened so Claude's codes are accepted more quickly
options.B: Claude's preliminary codes are accurate enough that the workflow is working as designed — 52% straight-through acceptance is reasonable for a complex clinical coding task
options.C: The 52% accept rate signals that Claude's code suggestions are frequently wrong or incomplete, meaning physicians spend most review time correcting rather than confirming — a sign the task may not be a good fit in its current form
options.D: The code assignments should be reviewed by a clinical coder rather than a physician to improve throughput

items.question: A lending operations manager at a regional bank automates the loan application pre-screening workflow: Claude reads each application, extracts income, assets, and debt-to-income ratio, compares against underwriting guidelines, and sends applicants a conditional approval or decline letter without human review. Within 30 days, the bank's compliance team flags two problems: (1) four applicants who should have qualified were declined based on a guideline Claude misinterpreted, and (2) the bank may have violated fair lending regulations by allowing an unreviewed AI to issue credit decisions. Which aspect of the design is the ROOT structural flaw?

options.A: The model used for pre-screening was not calibrated for financial services terminology
options.B: The workflow did not include a step to validate Claude's guideline interpretation against historical approvals before deployment
options.C: Claude was assigned to issue credit decision letters — a regulated, consequential output — without any human review, removing the accountability required by fair lending law
options.D: The income and asset extraction step should have been performed by the bank's core banking system rather than Claude

items.question: A content team at a pharmaceutical company designs a two-step AI workflow for medical education materials. Step 1: Claude summarises a 60-page clinical study into a 500-word lay summary. Step 2: a second Claude session takes the lay summary as input and generates questions for a physician training quiz. The team finds that the quiz questions are often too basic and do not adequately test clinical nuance. What is the MOST likely root cause?

options.A: The second Claude session should use a more capable model than the first
options.B: A 500-word lay summary, optimised for patient comprehension, loses the clinical detail that the second step needs to generate clinically nuanced quiz questions
options.C: Quiz generation should be done by a human subject-matter expert rather than Claude
options.D: The two steps should be combined into a single prompt to allow Claude to reference the full 60-page study when generating questions

items.question: A compliance team at an asset manager uses Claude to review 300 client communications per month for regulatory compliance flags. The team reviews Claude's flags and overrides about 15% of them. After six months, a regulator audit finds that the team had progressively raised the threshold for overriding Claude's non-flags — effectively becoming less likely to mark a communication as compliant if Claude had flagged it. The result is that true positives (genuinely non-compliant communications) that Claude missed were also missed by the team. What design failure does this scenario describe?

options.A: Claude's compliance detection criteria were not updated when the regulatory framework changed
options.B: The team did not have sufficient compliance expertise to override Claude's flags accurately
options.C: The workflow created automation bias: over time, the review team's oversight became anchored to Claude's output rather than exercising independent compliance judgment, causing missed non-flags to go undetected
options.D: A 15% override rate is too high, indicating Claude's flags were not reliable enough for production use

items.question: A grant administrator at a research university uses Claude to extract numerical data from 150 grant applications and compile the data into a comparison spreadsheet for the review committee. The committee identifies a grant that has been incorrectly ranked because Claude transposed a zero in one applicant's budget request ($1.2M read as $120K). The administrator uses a human review step but the error still reached the committee. What does this scenario MOST clearly illustrate about workflow design for numerical extraction tasks?

options.A: Claude should not be used for any tasks involving numerical data
options.B: A human review step is sufficient governance for numerical extraction tasks if the reviewer is given enough time
options.C: Numerical extraction errors are often invisible to reviewers who trust that an extracted figure is correct unless it strikes them as obviously implausible — the review step must be designed to catch transcription errors, not just logical errors
options.D: The comparison spreadsheet should have been generated by the grant management system, not Claude

items.question: A customer service operations manager at an insurance company uses Claude to triage 5,000 inbound emails per month, routing them to the appropriate team. The vast majority route correctly. However, a small number of emails contain implicit expressions of financial distress (customers mentioning they cannot pay premiums due to job loss) that require routing to a specialist team with vulnerability protocols. Claude routes these to the standard billing queue instead. What does this failure most clearly indicate about the workflow design?

options.A: Claude should be replaced by a human-only routing process for insurance email triage
options.B: The volume of 5,000 emails per month makes AI-assisted triage economically necessary, so the misrouting of vulnerable customers is an acceptable trade-off
options.C: The routing criteria were designed for high-frequency standard cases and did not include detection rules for low-frequency but high-consequence exception categories, creating a systematic gap for the most sensitive emails
options.D: The routing failure is a training data problem — Claude has not been exposed to enough examples of financially distressed customers

items.question: A financial analyst at a retail company runs a weekly batch workflow where Claude reads a Monday morning data extract and produces a commentary report on sales performance versus plan. This week's report contains incorrect variance calculations. The analyst investigates and finds the source system changed the column order in the extract file on Friday — plan figures are now in a different column. What does this failure illustrate about batch workflow resilience?

options.A: Claude cannot reliably perform mathematical calculations and should not be used for financial reporting
options.B: Batch workflows that depend on a fixed data format are fragile when upstream systems change their output structure — the workflow design should reference named columns or include a format validation step before processing
options.C: The prompt should have been written to handle any column order, since data formats inevitably change over time
options.D: The source system team should have notified the analyst before changing the column order

items.question: A communications manager at a 50-person non-profit successfully uses Claude to draft personalised thank-you letters to 30 major donors per quarter. Encouraged by this, she rolls out the same workflow to generate letters for all 4,000 annual donors. Three months later, the fundraising director reports a significant drop in re-donation rates. An analysis finds that the mass-generated letters contain no genuine personal detail — they feel formulaic. What does this illustrate about task suitability at different scales?

options.A: Claude writes lower-quality letters at high volume than at low volume due to processing constraints
options.B: The personalisation inputs (specific donor interactions, giving history, personal connection) that made the 30-letter workflow effective were not scalable to 4,000 donors — at scale, the letters lacked the information that made them personalised
options.C: Thank-you letters should always be handwritten and should never be AI-assisted at any scale
options.D: The fundraising director's analysis is anecdotal — a drop in re-donation rates cannot be attributed to letter quality alone

items.question: A research operations coordinator at a pharmaceutical company runs a three-step Claude workflow: (1) extract adverse events from 200 case narratives, (2) standardise extracted terms to MedDRA preferred terms, (3) compile a frequency summary table. In step 3, Claude produces a narrative summary instead of the structured table the downstream pharmacovigilance database requires. What is the MOST likely root cause and correct fix?

options.A: The model used in step 3 does not support structured output and should be replaced with an API-based structured output call
options.B: Step 3's prompt did not specify the required output format — adding explicit format instructions (column headers, row structure, delimiters) to the step 3 prompt should resolve the issue
options.C: Step 2's standardisation output was in the wrong format, causing step 3 to produce a narrative instead of a table
options.D: Multi-step workflows always require human review between steps to prevent format drift

items.question: An operations analyst at a logistics company builds a Claude workflow to summarise daily driver performance reports. Over three months, without formal redesign, the workflow scope expands: first to include fuel efficiency recommendations, then to flag potential driver disciplinary issues, then to include a preliminary HR note about each flagged driver. When the HR director discovers this, she immediately escalates to legal. What risk category does the scope expansion into HR notes MOST directly implicate?

options.A: Data accuracy risk — HR notes generated by AI may contain factual errors about individual drivers
options.B: Operational risk — the workflow is now more complex than originally designed and may have undocumented dependencies
options.C: Employment law and accountability risk — generating preliminary HR notes about individual employees without HR review or defined criteria creates an undocumented, AI-generated record with potential legal consequences in disciplinary proceedings
options.D: Data volume risk — adding HR notes to the daily report increases the output size beyond manageable review

items.question: A marketing operations manager at a SaaS company uses a Claude-based workflow to categorise 800 monthly sales inquiries into four lead types: enterprise, mid-market, SMB, and partner. The workflow has been stable for four months. A junior analyst updates the prompt to add "be concise" as a style instruction. The following week, the categorisation accuracy drops significantly and several enterprise leads are misclassified as SMB. What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.A: Adding style instructions to a classification prompt is always inappropriate and should never be done
options.B: The "be concise" instruction changed how Claude reasoned through the classification criteria — in truncating its reasoning, it may have skipped the steps that distinguished enterprise from SMB signals
options.C: The junior analyst should not have changed a production prompt without manager approval, which is a process violation unrelated to the prompt change itself
options.D: The categorisation task requires a more capable model to maintain accuracy with a shorter reasoning process

items.question: A content moderation team at a social platform uses a Claude-assisted workflow where Claude flags potentially policy-violating posts and a human moderator reviews each flag, marking each as "confirmed violation" or "false positive." After eight months, the team lead notices that the false positive rate has increased significantly. Investigation reveals two contributing factors. Which TWO factors would MOST plausibly explain the increased false positive rate? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The platform's policy language was tightened over six months, but the Claude prompt was not updated to reflect the narrower definitions
options.B: The human moderators became faster at reviewing flags over time as they gained experience
options.C: The moderator team composition changed, with several new reviewers who were more conservative in confirming violations, causing what had previously been confirmed violations to now be marked as false positives
options.D: Claude was updated to a newer version by the platform engineering team without updating the prompt to account for changed behaviour
options.E: The volume of posts reviewed per day doubled due to platform growth, increasing the absolute number of flags

items.question: A contract manager at a construction company uses Claude to review subcontractor agreements and flag clauses that conflict with the prime contract. For the first six months, the workflow works well. A new contract manager takes over and the workflow begins producing flags that experienced staff call "obviously wrong" — clauses flagged as conflicts that are actually aligned with the prime contract. Investigation reveals the previous manager always pasted the prime contract's key deviation clauses into the session before reviewing each subcontract. The new manager skips this step. What does this illustrate?

options.A: Claude's conflict-detection capability degrades over time without retraining
options.B: The workflow's effectiveness depended on undocumented context that was transferred through individual practice rather than embedded in the workflow design — when the practitioner changed, the context was lost
options.C: The new contract manager should receive more training on Claude before using the workflow
options.D: Contract review is too legally complex for AI assistance without a lawyer present

items.question: A pharmacist at a hospital pharmacy is evaluating a proposed Claude-assisted workflow that would read physician medication orders and highlight any that deviate from the hospital's formulary or dosing guidelines — with the pharmacist reviewing each highlight before dispensing. A colleague argues the workflow is inappropriate because drug-dosing errors are potentially fatal. The pharmacist believes the workflow is appropriate as designed. Which argument BEST supports the pharmacist's position?

options.A: Claude is highly accurate on pharmaceutical tasks and the error rate would be lower than manual review
options.B: The workflow uses Claude for flagging and highlighting, not for dispensing decisions — the pharmacist reviews every flag and makes all dispensing decisions independently, preserving human accountability for all patient-safety consequences
options.C: High-stakes tasks should always be done manually, and AI assistance introduces unacceptable risk regardless of how the workflow is designed
options.D: The colleague's concern is valid and the workflow should be abandoned in favour of a fully human review process

items.question: A programme director at a government agency wants to speed up a 12-week policy development cycle. A consultant proposes using Claude to summarise the 300 public consultation responses the agency receives. The programme director says this is not where the bottleneck is — the consultation analysis takes only 2 weeks, but the internal legal review of the draft policy takes 8 weeks. Where should Claude assistance MOST appropriately be focused to achieve the greatest time savings?

options.A: On summarising the consultation responses, since this is the most structured and repeatable part of the process
options.B: On replacing the legal review entirely, since 8 weeks of review is the obvious bottleneck
options.C: On preparing materials for the legal review — drafting structured issue summaries, flagging potential legal conflicts, and organising the policy document for reviewers — to reduce the preparation burden within the 8-week phase
options.D: On producing the final policy document, since drafting is a writing task Claude handles well

items.question: An insurance underwriting assistant uses Claude to produce a structured risk summary for each commercial property submission, which underwriters then use to make coverage and pricing decisions. An underwriter notices that the risk summaries consistently omit broker commentary — information brokers include in cover emails that often contains context about the property's history and the applicant's relationship with the broker. The broker emails arrive with each submission but the workflow only passes the formal application documents to Claude. What should the workflow designer do NEXT?

options.A: Accept the omission as a design choice — broker commentary is informal and may not be reliable
options.B: Update the workflow input to include the broker cover email alongside the formal application documents, and update the prompt to instruct Claude to extract and flag relevant broker commentary in the risk summary
options.C: Ask underwriters to add broker commentary manually to each risk summary after Claude generates it
options.D: Replace the Claude-generated summary with a fully human process so that underwriters can integrate all information sources directly

items.question: A safety engineer at an oil and gas company designs a Claude-assisted workflow to scan 4,000 maintenance work orders per month and flag any that describe conditions that could indicate a safety-critical defect. The workflow is calibrated to flag 8% of work orders for human safety review. An operations manager proposes recalibrating the workflow to flag only 4%, arguing that 8% is too many for the safety review team to handle. The safety engineer opposes this change. What is the safety engineer's STRONGEST argument?

options.A: Recalibration would require re-testing the entire prompt against a calibration dataset, which takes time
options.B: In safety-critical detection workflows, false negatives (genuine defects not flagged) are more dangerous than false positives (non-defects flagged for review) — reducing the flag rate saves review time but increases the risk of missing a real safety issue
options.C: The operations manager does not have the technical authority to change a safety workflow
options.D: The safety review team should be expanded rather than the flag rate reduced

items.question: A chief of staff at a 12,000-person bank is designing a regulatory reporting workflow. Each month, six analysts spend three days extracting data from five source systems and populating 22 mandated report templates. She wants to use Claude to accelerate this. After mapping the process, she identifies that 18 of the 22 templates are populated by extracting data against stable rules, but 4 templates require analyst judgment about how to classify edge cases under the regulator's guidance notes. How should she structure the Claude integration?

options.A: Apply Claude uniformly to all 22 templates — the efficiency gain is maximised when the full workflow is automated
options.B: Use Claude for the 18 rule-based templates as a first-draft and cross-check tool, preserve human analyst ownership of the 4 judgment templates, and establish a review step before any template is submitted
options.C: Use Claude only for the 4 judgment templates where its language understanding adds the most value, and keep the 18 rule-based templates with analysts
options.D: Automate all 22 templates and have a single senior analyst do a final pass review before submission

items.question: A clinical trial coordinator at a CRO needs to send 200 site activation letters to investigator sites before a study opens. Each letter must include the site's assigned patient enrolment target, the study drug shipment schedule, and the emergency contact for safety reporting. She plans to batch-generate all 200 letters using a data file and a template prompt. Her supervisor approves the efficiency gain but insists on a specific oversight structure. Which oversight design BEST balances efficiency with the regulatory requirement that site activation letters are accurate?

options.A: Batch-generate all 200 letters and send them directly to sites — the template ensures consistency
options.B: Batch-generate all 200 letters; have the coordinator review a random 10% sample; send the remainder without review
options.C: Batch-generate all 200 letters; have the coordinator and a second reviewer each review every letter before it is sent to the site
options.D: Batch-generate all 200 letters; have the coordinator review every letter against the source data file before sending, using a structured checklist to confirm enrolment target, shipment schedule, and emergency contact are correct for each site

items.question: A head of HR at a 2,000-person energy company receives 150 formal grievance filings per year. Each grievance requires: (1) initial triage to determine severity and urgency, (2) assignment to an investigator, (3) gathering supporting documentation, (4) drafting the investigation report, and (5) determination of outcome. A vendor proposes using Claude to assist with all five steps. Which assessment of this proposal is MOST accurate?

options.A: All five steps are appropriate for Claude assistance because the volume (150 per year) justifies automation
options.B: Steps 1 and 3 are appropriate for Claude assistance; steps 2, 4, and 5 are human-only
options.C: Steps 1, 3, and 4 are appropriate for Claude assistance as first-draft or preparation steps; steps 2 and 5 are human-only judgment and accountability steps
options.D: No steps are appropriate for Claude assistance because HR grievances are too sensitive for AI involvement

items.question: A strategy consultant is using Claude to produce a 40-page competitive analysis from 15 source documents (each 20–40 pages). She plans to read all 15 documents in a single conversation, have Claude synthesise findings, and draft the full report. A colleague warns that this approach risks producing inconsistent output. The consultant proposes an alternative: process each document separately to extract a structured summary, then draft the report from the 15 summaries in a separate session. Which aspect of the second approach MOST directly addresses the colleague's concern?

options.A: Separate sessions cost fewer tokens per session than one very long session
options.B: Extracting structured summaries first creates a stable, controlled intermediate layer — the report drafting session only receives the curated summaries, keeping the working context bounded and reducing the risk of early content being out of scope by the time the report is drafted
options.C: Two sessions are easier for the consultant to manage administratively than one very long session
options.D: The extraction session and the drafting session can run in parallel, reducing overall elapsed time

items.question: A compliance manager at a global bank uses Claude to assist with reviewing 600 monthly trade surveillance alerts. Analysts currently review each alert manually in about 12 minutes. The compliance manager proposes that Claude produce a preliminary analysis for each alert — reducing analyst review time to 4 minutes — with analysts making all final escalation decisions. The head of compliance approves the efficiency gain but requires that the audit trail show the analyst's independent assessment, not just a review of Claude's output. Which workflow design feature BEST satisfies this requirement?

options.A: The analyst records a timestamp showing when they reviewed Claude's preliminary analysis
options.B: The analyst completes a structured checklist of the alert's key risk factors independently before reading Claude's analysis, then records their independent assessment, Claude's analysis, and their final disposition decision in the audit log
options.C: The system logs Claude's preliminary analysis output alongside the analyst's final disposition in the audit trail
options.D: A second analyst reviews Claude's analysis for quality before the first analyst uses it

items.question: A business process analyst at a large retailer is designing a quarterly Claude-assisted workflow to analyse supplier performance. The workflow will process 180 suppliers, each with a data file containing quality metrics, delivery data, and pricing history. Which TWO design choices would MOST improve the reliability and efficiency of this batch workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Run all 180 supplier analyses in a single session to maintain context about cross-supplier comparisons
options.B: Define a standardised output schema for each supplier analysis (same sections, same field names, same scoring dimensions) so that outputs can be programmatically compiled into a comparison view
options.C: Process suppliers in batches of 20–30 per session, using the same standardised prompt for each batch to maintain consistency
options.D: Ask Claude to flag any suppliers where it is uncertain about a metric rather than generating a score it cannot confidently support
options.E: Have the category managers review Claude's analysis verbally with their teams rather than in writing to preserve flexibility in interpretation

items.question: A product manager at a fintech company is designing a workflow to process 5,000 customer loan applications per month. The workflow has five steps: (1) extract applicant data from the application form, (2) check the applicant against internal fraud flags, (3) compute a preliminary creditworthiness score using the company's scoring model, (4) generate a recommendation memo for the underwriter, and (5) underwriter review and final decision. She asks a senior consultant which of the five steps should use Claude. The consultant says: "Steps 1 and 4." Which reasoning BEST explains why steps 1 and 4, but not 2, 3, or 5?

options.A: Steps 1 and 4 involve text, while steps 2, 3, and 5 involve numbers and decisions
options.B: Step 1 is structured text extraction (high-fit); step 4 is structured synthesis into a narrative memo (high-fit); steps 2 and 3 require deterministic system outputs from validated models; step 5 is the accountable human decision
options.C: Steps 1 and 4 are the fastest steps so using Claude there has the most operational impact
options.D: Claude should be used in the first and last AI-compatible steps to act as a quality check on the middle steps

items.question: A benefits administrator at a 50,000-person manufacturer receives 4,000 employee benefit election forms annually during open enrolment. The process is highly repetitive: each form has the same structure, the same plan options, and the same eligibility rules. A vendor proposes fully automated processing — Claude reads each form, updates the benefits system, and sends the employee a confirmation, all without human review. The vendor argues the repetitiveness and volume make this a clear automation case. The benefits director pushes back. What is the STRONGEST argument for requiring at least some human review?

options.A: Claude may not be able to integrate with the benefits administration system's API
options.B: Benefit elections affect employees' health coverage, dependent coverage, and financial planning — an error in any individual employee's record has direct personal consequences that the employee may not discover until they try to use their coverage
options.C: 4,000 forms per year is not high enough volume to justify the investment in a fully automated workflow
options.D: The vendor has not demonstrated that Claude's form-reading accuracy is adequate for production deployment

items.question: An environmental compliance manager at a chemical plant uses Claude to scan 80 monthly inspection reports and flag any that describe conditions that may violate the plant's operating permit. A regulator visits and reviews three months of flagged reports. The regulator notes that while the flagged reports are well-documented, there is no evidence that the compliance team independently assessed unflagged reports. The manager argues that the team reviews all flags thoroughly. What is the regulator's concern?

options.A: The flags are insufficient in number to satisfy the regulatory expectation of thorough permit compliance monitoring
options.B: The compliance team's review is limited to items Claude surfaces — if Claude systematically misses a category of permit violation, no human review catches it, creating a surveillance blind spot
options.C: The inspection reports should be stored in a format accessible to the regulator, not processed by an AI system
options.D: The compliance manager has not documented Claude's accuracy rate, which the regulator needs to assess the adequacy of the monitoring system

items.question: A research analyst at an asset management firm uses a three-step Claude workflow: Step 1 extracts financial metrics from 30 earnings call transcripts. Step 2 uses Step 1's output to identify trends across the 30 companies. Step 3 uses Step 2's output to draft an investment thesis paragraph. The analyst notices the final thesis paragraph contains an incorrect revenue growth figure that propagated from Step 1 through Step 2 into Step 3. Which TWO design changes would MOST effectively prevent this type of error propagation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Add a human verification step after Step 1, confirming extracted figures against source transcripts before Step 2 runs
options.B: Combine all three steps into a single prompt so Claude can self-correct across the full workflow
options.C: Run Step 1 with a structured output format that includes source citation for each extracted figure, enabling spot-check verification before Step 2
options.D: Use a more capable model in Step 1 to improve extraction accuracy
options.E: Design Step 3 to include a final data check, comparing the thesis paragraph figures against the Step 1 extraction output before approving

items.question: A tax manager at a professional services firm uses Claude to draft the tax commentary sections for 200 client tax returns annually. Each section is 1–2 pages. The partner in charge of quality approves the workflow but requires that it be "audit ready" — meaning a reviewer can demonstrate exactly why any tax position was taken. Which feature of the workflow design is MOST critical for audit readiness?

options.A: Each commentary draft is stored with a timestamp so the review order can be reconstructed
options.B: The workflow records which version of Claude and which prompt version generated each commentary, alongside the source documents used and the reviewing partner's sign-off with their changes
options.C: The same prompt is used for all 200 commentaries to ensure consistency
options.D: The commentaries are reviewed by two partners rather than one for high-stakes clients

items.question: A three-person research team at an NGO produces an annual global health situation report — a 120-page document drawing on 400 source publications. Historically this takes 18 months from kickoff to publication. The team wants to use Claude to reduce the cycle to 9 months. A consultant maps the current timeline and finds: literature search and screening (3 months), evidence synthesis (6 months), writing (5 months), expert review and revision (4 months). Where should Claude assistance be focused FIRST to have the greatest impact on cycle time?

options.A: The writing phase, because Claude can draft 120 pages much faster than three people
options.B: The literature search and screening phase, because automating it would eliminate the first three months
options.C: The evidence synthesis phase, because at 6 months it is the longest single phase and compressing it would have the greatest overall cycle time impact
options.D: The expert review phase, because experts are the external bottleneck and Claude can pre-process submissions to speed their review

items.question: A director of clinical operations at a hospital is designing a new patient discharge workflow with three proposed Claude-assisted elements: (A) generating a structured medication reconciliation checklist from the patient chart; (B) drafting a plain-language discharge summary for the patient from the clinical notes; (C) producing a preliminary decision on whether the patient should be discharged today or observed for another 24 hours. A hospitalist physician reviews the proposal. Which elements should the physician APPROVE for Claude assistance and which should be REJECTED?

options.A: Approve A and C; reject B because patient-facing documents require physician authorship
options.B: Approve A and B; reject C because the discharge-vs-observation decision is a clinical judgment with patient-safety consequences that must be made by the attending physician
options.C: Approve A, B, and C because all three are draft outputs that a physician reviews before implementation
options.D: Reject A, B, and C because clinical workflows should not include AI assistance due to patient safety risk

items.question: A head of operations at a 150-person professional services firm is evaluating three proposed Claude-assisted workflows before approving deployment. Workflow 1: Claude drafts client engagement letters from a template, reviewed by the client partner before sending. Workflow 2: Claude analyses 500 internal expense reports per month and flags potential policy violations, with a finance analyst reviewing all flags. Workflow 3: Claude automatically approves and processes employee expense claims below £50 with no human review. Which TWO workflows should be APPROVED without modification? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Workflow 1, because drafting client letters with partner review is an appropriate draft-and-review pattern
options.B: Workflow 2, because flagging policy violations with analyst review maintains human accountability for the compliance decision
options.C: Workflow 3, because £50 claims are low-stakes and the volume justifies automation
options.D: Workflow 1 and 3, because both have clear efficiency gains
options.E: Workflow 2 and 3, because both handle high volume and repetitive inputs

items.question: A COO at a 500-person insurance company has approved a project to redesign three high-volume workflows using Claude: (1) policy renewal letters (12,000 per year, templated, reviewed by agents), (2) claims triage (8,000 per month, Claude flags for specialist routing, human adjuster reviews all flags), and (3) actuarial assumption memos (200 per year, Claude drafts from data tables, reviewed and signed by a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries). After six months, the project manager reports that all three are performing well on efficiency metrics. The COO asks what the NEXT governance action should be to ensure sustained performance. What should the project manager recommend?

options.A: Expand the automation scope by removing the agent review from policy renewal letters, since the accept-without-change rate is 91%
options.B: Establish ongoing performance monitoring for each workflow — tracking accept rates, override reasons, and a periodic sample review of non-flagged items in claims triage — and set thresholds that trigger a prompt or workflow review if metrics drift
options.C: Declare the project complete and reallocate the project team to new automation initiatives
options.D: Switch to a more capable model tier for the actuarial memos to further reduce the Fellow's revision time

items.question: A head of procurement at a global manufacturing company is designing a Claude-assisted vendor onboarding workflow. The process handles 300 new vendors annually. Steps: (1) extract structured information from vendor application forms, (2) screen vendor names against a sanctions list, (3) assess vendor financial health from submitted balance sheets, (4) generate a risk summary for the procurement committee, and (5) make the formal vendor approval decision. Which TWO steps should NOT use Claude as the primary or sole automated actor? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Step 1: extracting structured data from vendor application forms
options.B: Step 2: screening vendor names against a sanctions list
options.C: Step 3: assessing vendor financial health from submitted balance sheets
options.D: Step 4: generating a risk summary for the procurement committee
options.E: Step 5: making the formal vendor approval decision

items.question: A policy analyst at a government ministry uses Claude daily to assist with briefing notes, Parliamentary questions, and policy correspondence. She uses a single long-running conversation that she has maintained for four months, adding to it every day. A colleague notices that Claude's briefing notes from week 16 reference a policy position that was superseded in week 8. What is the MOST likely explanation for this inconsistency?

options.A: Claude stores and recalls all previous conversation content accurately but selected an older position for stylistic reasons
options.B: The four-month conversation has accumulated enough content that early weeks' context is no longer reliably in scope when new briefings are generated, causing Claude to revert to earlier stated positions
options.C: The colleague is mistaken — Claude does not retain information across sessions and treats each conversation turn independently
options.D: Parliamentary policy positions should be tracked in a system of record, not in a Claude conversation, which is a separate issue from the inconsistency

items.question: A managing director at a financial advisory firm is designing a client-facing workflow where Claude drafts personalised investment suitability assessments from a structured fact-find questionnaire. The firm's compliance officer approves the workflow but specifies: "the assessment must be attributable to a named financial adviser, not to the AI." Which workflow design feature BEST satisfies this requirement?

options.A: The AI system discloses in the document footer that the assessment was generated with AI assistance
options.B: The financial adviser reviews Claude's draft, makes any necessary amendments, and signs off with their adviser code before the assessment is sent to the client — making the signed document unambiguously their professional output
options.C: The assessment is sent from the adviser's email address rather than a generic firm address
options.D: The firm's AI governance committee approves the prompt template used to generate all assessments

items.question: A data protection officer at a 10,000-person retail company deploys Claude to assist with reviewing Data Subject Access Requests (DSARs). Claude reads each DSAR, identifies which data categories are likely held, and drafts a response letter — reviewed and signed off by the DPO or a deputy before sending. After 3 months, a DSAR arrives from an individual who is also a party to active litigation against the company. Claude drafts a standard response. The DPO escalates immediately. Why is this specific DSAR an exception to the standard workflow?

options.A: DSARs from individuals in litigation are exempt from data protection law and should be declined automatically
options.B: The DSAR process was designed for routine requests; a DSAR from a litigation party creates a legal privilege, legal hold, and disclosure risk intersection that requires legal counsel review before any response is drafted or sent
options.C: Claude should have identified the litigation connection and flagged this DSAR automatically
options.D: The DPO review step is sufficient to catch this exception — the escalation is unnecessary since the DPO reviews every letter before sending

items.question: A VP of Operations at a 25,000-person logistics company has run a 90-day pilot of Claude-assisted workflows across four business units: (1) freight invoice audit (high-volume, rule-based, 92% accept rate), (2) customer contract drafting (moderate volume, templated, 78% accept rate, reviewed by account managers), (3) customs documentation for cross-border shipments (structured form completion, 85% accept rate, reviewed by a licensed customs broker), and (4) driver scheduling recommendations (variable, complex, 61% accept rate). After reviewing the pilot results, which workflow requires the MOST immediate design intervention before broader rollout?

options.A: Workflow 1, because freight invoice processing involves financial data requiring tighter governance
options.B: Workflow 2, because customer contracts are legally binding and should have lawyer review rather than account manager review
options.C: Workflow 4, because a 61% accept rate indicates that driver scheduling recommendations require significant reviewer correction — the workflow is not delivering reliable enough output to justify broader rollout without redesign
options.D: Workflow 3, because customs documentation errors can result in shipment delays and regulatory penalties

items.question:
A bank's compliance team uses Claude to flag transactions that may require a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing. Reviewing the workflow diagram, a senior analyst notices that after Claude flags a transaction it is automatically routed to the SAR filing queue with no human step in between.

What is the MOST significant risk this design creates?

options.A: Claude may fail to flag some qualifying transactions, creating coverage gaps in the bank's AML programme.
options.B: The workflow creates straight-through processing of a high-stakes regulatory output, meaning any error in Claude's assessment becomes a filed SAR with no human able to catch it.
options.C: Claude's structured output may not map cleanly to the SAR filing system's required data fields without a validated connector.
options.D: Compliance analysts may lose proficiency in manual transaction review if Claude handles all initial flagging.

items.question:
A bid manager at a public-sector consulting firm uses Claude to draft responses to government RFPs. The current workflow is: Claude generates the draft, a colleague performs a grammar and formatting check, and the draft is sent to the client. A new internal policy requires an approval gate to be added.

Where should the approval gate MOST appropriately be placed?

options.A: After the grammar and formatting check, immediately before client submission — ensuring a reviewed draft is authorised before it leaves the organisation.
options.B: Before Claude begins drafting, so a senior partner can approve the bid strategy before any content is generated.
options.C: After client submission, to review the client's response and decide whether to proceed.
options.D: Immediately after Claude generates the draft, before the grammar check, so the approver sees the raw AI output.

items.question:
An HR business partner at a large retail company uses Claude to help draft performance improvement plans (PIPs). The CHRO instructs the team to save each Claude-assisted PIP with a timestamp, the prompt used, and the name of the HR partner who reviewed it — before sharing it with the affected employee.

Which governance principle does this documentation practice PRIMARILY support?

options.A: Data minimisation — fewer personal details captured in the prompt reduce the privacy exposure of sensitive employee information.
options.B: Least-privilege access — only HR partners can view the PIP record, limiting who can act on the information it contains.
options.C: Auditability — the record establishes who authorised the AI-assisted output and when, enabling the organisation to demonstrate responsible oversight if challenged.
options.D: Version control — multiple draft iterations can be compared against the final PIP to trace how it evolved.

items.question:
A telecoms company deploys a Claude-powered chatbot to handle billing queries. When Claude cannot reliably resolve a query — for example, a complex international roaming dispute — the chatbot transfers the conversation to a human agent with a summary of what has been discussed.

What workflow pattern does this behaviour BEST illustrate?

options.A: An approval gate that pauses processing until a senior agent authorises the resolution.
options.B: A connector that synchronises conversation history with the CRM before escalation.
options.C: A human-in-the-loop checkpoint that is triggered at a fixed interval regardless of query complexity.
options.D: A fallback path that activates when the AI reaches the boundary of its reliable capability, routing the interaction to a human with context preserved.

items.question:
A hospital's clinical operations team uses Claude to draft discharge summaries from structured EMR data. Two workflow designs are proposed:

**Design X:** Claude drafts the summary; the attending physician reviews and approves it before it is written to the EMR.
**Design Y:** Claude drafts the summary; a ward clerk reviews it for formatting and completeness before it is written to the EMR.

Which design BEST satisfies the requirement for a clinically appropriate review checkpoint?

options.A: Design X, because only a clinician qualified in the patient's care can vouch for the clinical accuracy of a discharge summary before it becomes a permanent medical record.
options.B: Design Y, because the ward clerk is closer to the daily workflow and can respond faster, reducing the time discharge summaries spend in the queue.
options.C: Design X, but only if the physician receives the draft within 30 minutes of discharge so the clinical detail is still fresh.
options.D: Design Y, because clerical review catches formatting errors that could cause downstream processing problems in the EMR.
